doc_name: List of solar eclipses in the 19th century
text: During the 19th century, there were 242 solar eclipses, consisting of 87 partial, 77 annular, 63 total, and 15 hybrid eclipses (which are a combination of total and annular). The highest number of eclipses in a single year was five, occurring in 1805, while the years 1801, 1812, 1819, 1823, 1830, 1841, 1848, 1859, 1870, and 1880 each had four eclipses. Two months, January 1805 and December 1880, each contained two solar eclipses: on January 1 and January 30, 1805, and on December 2 and December 31, 1880. These predictions were provided by Fred Espenak of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center. The longest duration of totality, when the Moon fully covered the Sun, occurred on August 7, 1850, with a maximum duration of 6 minutes and 50 seconds; the longest possible duration for a total solar eclipse is 7 minutes and 32 seconds. The longest annular solar eclipse of the century happened on October 30, 1883, lasting 10 minutes and 17 seconds, with a maximum possible duration of 12 minutes and 29 seconds. Four instances of back-to-back hybrid solar eclipses within less than six months occurred in the 19th century: the first on June 6 and November 29, 1807; the second on June 16 and December 9, 1825; the third on October 20, 1827, and April 14, 1828; and the fourth on October 30, 1845, and April 25, 1846. The table lists the date and time of the greatest eclipse in dynamical time (equivalent to Ephemeris Time), the saros series number, the eclipse type (total, annular, partial, or hybrid), the gamma value (indicating how centrally the Moon's shadow hits Earth), and the magnitude (the fraction of the Sun's diameter obscured by the Moon). For total and annular eclipses, the duration, location of the greatest eclipse, and path width are included, along with the geographical areas where the eclipse is visible and a chart showing each eclipse's path.
